title: Describing people
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: huwa and hiya are the free pronouns for he and she. L1 never needed them, because the ya-/ta- prefix already carried the person inside the verb — they arrive now because a sentence with no verb has nowhere else to put it.
There is still no copula. huwa ṭawīl is two words and means "he is tall", exactly as anā ṭālib did in the first module of the course.
The possessive suffixes continue: -ī mine, -ka yours (m), -ki yours (f), -hu his, and now -hā hers. They attach with no hyphen and no space, so each suffixed shape is its own word.

ʿind- is not a verb. It is a preposition meaning "at", which is why it takes the possessive suffixes rather than conjugating — ʿindī, ʿindaka, ʿindahā — and why Arabic has no verb "to have" to look for.
Two nouns in a row is possession: bayt ṣadīqī, "my friend's house". The FIRST noun never takes al-, however definite the phrase is.
An adjective agrees with what it describes: huwa ṭawīl, hiya ṭawīla. That is the same law the course has applied since ṭālib and ṭāliba, now with a pronoun in front of it.

sentences.cue: He is a student at the school

words.note: The free pronoun for he. L1 never needed it, because a verb's ya- prefix already said who; a sentence with no verb has nowhere else to put the person.

sentences.trap: No word for "is" and none for "a". Three Arabic words carry six English ones, and both missing pieces are the same absence L1-M1 taught.
sentences.sound: HU-wa, and the w is fully said — it is not the vowel of English "who".

variations.cue: He is a teacher at the school
variations.changed: a different job in the same building
an adjective instead of a place
hal in front turns it into a question and moves nothing

mistake.why: There is no "is" to add. huwa ṭālib is the whole sentence, and repeating the pronoun is what an English speaker does looking for the verb.

sentences.usage: Introducing someone who is not present. With someone standing there, hādhā is warmer.
sentences.mnemonic: The sentence is finished before you have looked for the verb.

sentences.cue: She is a teacher at the school

words.note: The partner of huwa, and the two differ by one letter in the script as well as in the sound. Neither carries any hint of an "is".

sentences.trap: mudarrisa and al-madrasa look alike and are unrelated: one is a teacher, the other a school. Arabic builds both from the same three letters and gives them different shapes.
sentences.sound: HI-ya. mu-DAR-ri-sa, with the r doubled and held.

variations.cue: She is a student at the school
variations.changed: the feminine of ṭālib, which L1-M1 already taught
an adjective, agreeing with her
asked as a question

mistake.why: A woman is a mudarrisa. The -a is not optional, and L1-M2 taught the pair.

sentences.usage: The same introduction, about a woman. Both pronouns are used far less in speech than in writing, because a verb usually says who.
sentences.mnemonic: One letter apart in the script, and a whole person apart in the room.

sentences.cue: Her name is Hind and she is beautiful

words.note: ism with -hā glued on, exactly as ismuhu (M1) took -hu. The suffix attaches with no space, so this is one word and one index key.

sentences.trap: -hā for her, -hu for him, and no space before either. English writes "her name" as two words and Arabic writes one.
sentences.sound: IS-mu-hā, with the long ā at the end carrying no stress of its own.

variations.changed: the masculine suffix, which M1 taught

variations.cue: Her name is Hind and she is a student
variations.changed: a noun instead of an adjective after wa

variations.cue: My name is Rohan and her name is Hind
variations.changed: two suffixes on the same word, side by side

mistake.why: The suffix is part of the word: ismuhā. Arabic never leaves a possessive pronoun standing apart.

sentences.usage: Introducing a third person. wa joins the two halves and is written joined to the word after it.
sentences.mnemonic: Every possessive in Arabic arrives glued.

words.note: Literally "at her". ʿind- is a preposition, which is why it takes suffixes rather than conjugating — and why the past is kāna ʿindahā, with kāna doing the tense.

sentences.trap: "ʿindī means I have" is memorable and useless: it leaves you unable to explain ʿindahā, or the past, or why there is no verb. ʿind- is "at", and Arabic locates a thing at a person.
sentences.sound: ʿIN-da-hā, with the ʿayn tightening the throat before the first vowel.

variations.changed: the masculine suffix, and a different adjective

variations.cue: She has a house near the school
variations.changed: something bigger, and a place named
asked of a man, with M7's own suffix

mistake.why: The suffix already says who. Adding hiya in front is the English shape, and it reads as insistence.

sentences.usage: Everyday possession. The adjective follows the noun, as it always does in this course.
sentences.mnemonic: Arabic has nothing; it only ever has things AT it.

sentences.cue: He is tall and she is short

words.note: Tall of a person and long of a thing alike. The ṭ is emphatic — a t said with the tongue flattened and the whole mouth darker.
The opposite of ṭawīl, agreeing with her. The q is made far back in the throat, and the ṣ is emphatic like the ṭ.

sentences.trap: Two clauses, two pronouns, two adjectives, and every ending is decided by the person it belongs to. Nothing here agrees with the speaker.
sentences.sound: ṭa-WĪL, qa-ṢĪ-ra — both stressed on the long ī.

variations.cue: He is short and she is tall
variations.changed: the two swapped, and both endings follow
one clause, with jiddan intensifying
the same adjective describing a thing

mistake.why: The adjective agrees with hiya: qaṣīra. Agreement does not stop at the first clause.

sentences.usage: Plain description, and Arabic is comfortable making it about someone present.
sentences.mnemonic: Each half of the sentence answers to its own person.

sentences.cue: I have a brother and a sister

words.note: Two letters and one syllable. The kh is the sound at the end of Scottish "loch", made at the back of the mouth.
The feminine of akh, and unusually it does not simply add -a: the vowel changes too. Learn the pair rather than deriving one from the other.

sentences.trap: ukht is not akha. This is one of the few family words where the feminine is a different shape rather than an ending.
sentences.sound: AKH and UKHT, both one syllable, and the kh is the same in each.

variations.cue: I have a brother in Egypt
variations.changed: a place, from M9 of the level below

variations.cue: She has a brother and a sister
variations.changed: the same family, someone else's
asked of a man

mistake.why: The word for sister is ukht, not a feminine built off akh.

sentences.usage: The first question anyone asks a newcomer in an Arabic-speaking country, and the first answer they give.
sentences.mnemonic: Two letters for a brother, three for a sister, and a new vowel in between.

sentences.cue: This is my father and this is my mother

words.note: ab with -ī glued on. The bare word for father almost never appears alone in speech; it arrives already owned by somebody.
umm with -ī. The m is doubled and held, which is what separates it from the preposition min in the ear.

sentences.trap: hādhā for him and hādhihi for her. The pointing word agrees with what is pointed at, which is the same law as every adjective in the course.
sentences.sound: a-BĪ and um-MĪ, both stressed on the long ī at the end.

variations.cue: This is my father and he is a teacher
variations.changed: a job added after the introduction

variations.cue: This is my mother and she is beautiful
variations.changed: the feminine half on its own
the same person described rather than introduced

mistake.why: A woman is pointed at with hādhihi. The pointing word agrees like everything else.

sentences.usage: Introducing family to a guest, and it is done in exactly this order.
sentences.mnemonic: Parents arrive already belonging to someone.

sentences.cue: My friend's house is near the school

words.note: ṣadīq with -ī. The ṣ is emphatic and the q is made at the back of the throat, so the whole word sits low in the mouth.

sentences.trap: bayt has no al- in front of it, and the phrase is still definite: "THE house of my friend". The second noun's ownership makes the first one definite, and adding al- would break it.
sentences.sound: ṣa-DĪ-qī, and the q is not a k — it is made further back and lower.

variations.cue: My father's house is near the market
variations.changed: another owner and another landmark
a different thing owned, and the tāʾ shows in the script

variations.cue: My mother's house is near the market
variations.changed: the same two-noun frame with another owner

mistake.why: The first noun of a two-noun possession never takes al-: bayt ṣadīqī.

sentences.usage: Everyday. It is how Arabic says anything belongs to anyone, and it costs no extra word at all.
sentences.mnemonic: The second noun makes the first one definite, so the al- is not needed.

words.note: Warm and easy to be around, said of people and of weather alike. The ṭ is emphatic, which darkens the vowel around it.

sentences.trap: jiddan goes AFTER the adjective. English puts "very" in front and Arabic puts it behind, every time.
sentences.sound: la-ṬĪF, with the ṭ pulling the a towards an o.

variations.changed: the feminine, and the adjective follows her
two adjectives joined by wa
the same word about the weather, with M5's al-jaww

mistake.why: jiddan follows what it intensifies: laṭīf jiddan. Putting it in front is the English order.

sentences.usage: The default compliment about a person's character, and it is used constantly.
sentences.mnemonic: Arabic puts its very at the back.

words.note: Arabic says someone is big IN AGE rather than old. The s is a sun letter, so al- assimilates: as-sinn, written السن and said with a doubled s.

sentences.trap: kabīra alone would mean she is big. The fī as-sinn is what turns size into age, and it cannot be left off.
sentences.sound: as-SINN, with the l of al- swallowed entirely into the s and the s held long.

variations.changed: the masculine, and the adjective follows him
a named person instead of a pronoun
kabīra without fī as-sinn, which means size again

mistake.why: s is a sun letter, so the l assimilates: as-sinn. The build treats al-sinn and as-sinn as two different words.

sentences.usage: Said with respect rather than as a plain fact. Arabic has no comfortable equivalent of the blunt English "old".
sentences.mnemonic: Big in the age, not old.

comprehensionPool.cue: He is a student at the school
She is a teacher at the school
Her name is Hind and she is beautiful
He is tall and she is short
I have a brother and a sister
This is my father and this is my mother
My friend's house is near the school
